papers.title: Qwen-Audio-3.1-ASR Technical Report
papers.abstract: We present Qwen-Audio-3.1-ASR, a family of audio-language models that builds upon its predecesor Qwen-Audio-3.0-ASR with improved speech recognition and expanded capabilities in speaker-diarized transcription and general audio understanding. The family retains support for 30 languages and 16 Chinese dialects, together with instruction-controlled capabilities including historical-context conditioning, hierarchical hotword customization, and native transcription polishing. Speaker-diarized ASR produces structured outputs containing speaker labels, timestamps, and recognized text, maintaining consistent speaker labels across turns and the representation of overlapping speech. The general audio understanding capabilities cover audio-, speech-, and music-captioning, temporal grounding and sound event detection, as well as audio question answering and multiple-choice reasoning. These tasks broaden the application scope from recognizing spoken words to interpreting speakers, acoustic events, and their temporal relations. To accommodate different deployment requirements, the family includes variants for asynchronous file transcription, low-latency streaming, interactive voice input, and non-streaming recognition, with speaker-diarized transcription and general audio understanding available in certain variants. Evaluations span conventional ASR, multilingual and dialectal speech, speaker-diarized transcription, and general audio understanding, demonstrating the capabilities of the Qwen-Audio-3.1-ASR family across transcription and broader audio analysis tasks.

papers.title: Heard But Not Said: Prompting Understates Temporal Information of Musical Moments in Frozen Large Audio-Language Models
papers.abstract: Large audio-language models (LALMs) understand music, yet struggle to locate a described moment in time. We ask whether this reflects missing temporal information or a bottleneck in how the time span is extracted. Using a paired-query probe built from Slakh2100 stem activations, we attach a state query (e.g., ``only piano and bass are playing'') and a change query (e.g., ``the guitar drops out, leaving piano and bass'') to the same span and vary how much preceding audio the model is shown. Across frozen LALMs, three ways of extracting the span ask different questions: full-track prompting asking whether the model can say when; windowed yes/no scoring asking whether it verifies the moment when handed the segment, and whether it needs what came before; attention asking whether it can find the moment on its own. State queries score above baseline without context, while change queries improve with preceding context in most short-segment models; 30s padded encoders show no comparable recovery. Prompting and attention expose almost none of this. Prompting failures thus understate what LALMs can verify, though not what they can locate, by an amount set by query type and encoder.

papers.title: Character-Level Prosody Control for Mandarin Speech Synthesis:An Architecture-Preserving Approach
papers.abstract: This paper addresses fine-grained prosody control for large-language-model (LLM) based text-to-speech (TTS) synthesis of Mandarin Chinese, motivated by multimedia content-creation scenarios---film dubbing, audiobook production, and interactive voice interfaces---in which prosodic adjustments must be placed on specific characters rather than applied uniformly to whole utterances. We present a data-driven framework in which fine-grained prosodic markers (pitch, duration, energy, and pause) are automatically extracted from raw audio at scale and embedded into the text stream as out-of-vocabulary Unicode symbols. The LLM of an existing TTS system is then fine-tuned to interpret these markers while its architecture remains unchanged, yielding character-level temporal control that complements existing utterance-level style control. An optional text-LLM front-end can translate natural-language instructions into marker sequences. Experiments on 2.15M Mandarin utterances (5,858 hours) with CosyVoice2 as the backbone demonstrate reliable control of character duration, pitch, pause duration, and global speaking rate, with perceptual quality essentially preserved. A cross-tokenizer analysis further indicates that the ASR-optimized tokenizer of the backbone attenuates prosodic variation relative to reconstruction-oriented alternatives---an observation we report as hypothesis-generating evidence for prosody-sensitive system design.

papers.title: RubatoCodec: Budgeted Adaptive Speech Tokenization with Streaming Decoding
papers.abstract: Neural speech codecs provide discrete tokens for speech generation. Lower frame rates shorten token sequences, but each token must then carry more linguistic and acoustic information. Variable-frame-rate codecs address this trade-off by adapting token allocation to speech content, but threshold-based allocation lets content determine the token count, so the sequence length a speech generator must produce varies across utterances and datasets at a fixed setting. We present RubatoCodec, a variable-frame-rate speech codec built on X-Codec-2 with an exact utterance-level event budget and streaming decoding. Its Adaptive Firing mechanism uses changes in codec features and waveform spectra to divide speech into variable-duration events without a learned boundary predictor. Discrete codes and an explicit duration represent each event, allowing a speech generator to predict and decode one event at a time. Controlled experiments show that adaptive allocation outperforms fixed-rate coding in reconstruction fidelity and intelligibility at low event rates. A model trained on large-scale multilingual speech achieves competitive reconstruction quality across English, Japanese, and Mandarin, with the best intelligibility preservation among the compared codecs on the evaluated English and Japanese benchmarks at comparable bitrates. In a matched text-to-speech comparison, the adaptive representation yields lower WER and higher UTMOS and UTMOSv2 with comparable speaker similarity. The speech generator also learns the codec's utterance-level event budget without an explicit generation-time rate constraint. These results demonstrate that budgeted adaptive speech representations support both high-quality reconstruction and streaming text-to-speech generation. Code and weights are available at https://github.com/third-intelligence/RubatoCodec and https://huggingface.co/third-intelligence/RubatoCodec.
reasons: Speech Generation, Recognition & Dialogue: speech generation, text-to-speech

papers.title: Closed-Loop Dual-Reference Guidance for Accent Control in Cross-Lingual Voice Cloning
papers.abstract: Zero-shot cross-lingual voice cloning often carries the reference speaker's accent into the target language. We propose closed-loop dual-reference guidance, which pairs the original reference with a reusable native anchor constructed by voice conversion (VC). The references initialize separate language-model (LM) states that guide a shared acoustic trajectory; each completed patch then updates both states, keeping their generated histories aligned with the emitted speech. Anchor construction runs once per speaker, and online synthesis uses a frozen TTS model without per-utterance VC. On 20 held-out French speakers, the fixed setting $\lambda^{\!*}=0.33$ reduces residual French LID mass by 73\% versus direct cloning, at an ECAPA similarity cost of only $0.042$; relative to anchor-only cloning, it recovers $0.155$. The method achieves the lowest mean WER ($0.009$) and highest mean GOP ($4.750$) among the held-out test arms. In blinded preference tests, native-English listeners favor it over direct cloning on pronunciation naturalness, and over both anchor-only cloning and a TTS$\to$VC cascade on speaker identity. Online RTF is approximately 26\% lower than the cascade's ($0.59$ vs.\ $0.80$), and the same setting reduces Spanish LID mass by 56\% without re-tuning.
reasons: Speech Generation, Recognition & Dialogue: voice cloning

papers.title: NeuroCodec: EEG-Guided Latent-Domain Generative Model for High-Fidelity Target Speaker Extraction
papers.abstract: Driven by recent advancements in hearing assistive devices, target speaker extraction (TSE) in multi-talker environments has drawn significant attention. To address this, hearing technologies identify attention using neural signals recorded via electroencephalography (EEG) to guide TSE, enabling neuro-steered auditory attention decoding. However, most existing techniques rely on time-frequency masking, which suffers from low fidelity in spectro-temporally overlapping regions and is often restricted to narrowband audio. In contrast, we introduce NeuroCodec, which, to the best of our knowledge, is the first generative EEG-guided TSE framework operating in the latent space of a neural audio codec. Specifically, NeuroCodec models spatial EEG dependencies via graph convolutions and fuses cross-modal EEG and speech representations through attention mechanisms and Mamba-based temporal modeling. We further introduce a six-phase training curriculum that progressively incorporates latent reconstruction, multi-scale spectral, and adversarial objectives to ensure stable, high-fidelity speech generation. Experiments on the public Cocktail Party and KUL datasets show NeuroCodec outperforms baselines, across several perceptual metrics. A listening experiment with 20 participants validated that NeuroCodec offers greater perceptual accuracy, achieving a mean score of 82.24 compared with 49.63 for M3ANet. Additionally, the proposed method is seen to enable 44.1 kHz reconstruction with spectral content extending up to 20 kHz, further supporting the perceptual results. Finally, we extend NeuroCodec with a causal streaming formulation suited for real-time processing, providing a basis for hearing assistive devices.

papers.title: Derivation Depth Exposes Reasoning Failures in Tool-Augmented Music Analysis
papers.abstract: Audio-language models remain unreliable at extracting basic musical properties from audio, motivating pipelines that place a music information retrieval (MIR) tool between the audio and the model. The tool reports measurements such as keys, chords, and structural similarity, and the model is expected to derive the answer. We test whether it can. Holding the musical information fixed, we vary derivation depth: the number of reasoning steps between the tool output and the answer. When the report states the conclusion, all five models score near 100%, and they follow it even when it is wrong. One step away, accuracy drops. On modulation, open models fall to 57-81%, although they answer that single step correctly when asked directly, and reach 0% at greater depths. Frontier models degrade less, but still degrade. Adding the audio does not recover the loss. The bottleneck in tool-augmented music analysis is not access to musical information but reasoning from it, so tool design must account for how much derivation it leaves to the model.
reasons: Audio & Speech Language Models: audio-language model
Music Foundation Models & Representations: music information retrieval

papers.title: XingChen-UniFE: A Unified Generative Speech Front-End via Complementary Acoustic-Semantic Modeling
papers.abstract: This paper presents XingChen-UniFE, a unified large audio language model (LALM) for general speech restoration (GSR) and target speaker extraction (TSE). The proposed model employs complementary semantic and acoustic representations through a dual-stream encoder, where a self-supervised learning model provides hierarchical semantic features and a learnable acoustic branch captures fine-grained structures from complex spectra. A bidirectional cross-attention module further facilitates information exchange between the two representations. The fused representation conditions the LALM for discrete speech token generation with task and speaker information. Experiments demonstrate strong performance on both GSR and TSE and robust generalization to unseen degradation conditions.

Ming-3.0-audio-flash

Hear clearly. Understand deeply. Act intelligently.

Ming-3.0-audio-flash is a native audio-language model from inclusionAI. It accepts audio together with text instructions and supports speech recognition, spoken question answering, audio understanding, audio reasoning, and optional synthesized-speech responses.
GitHub · 🤖 ModelScope · 🤗 Flash · 🤗 Tiny · 💻 Examples
## Model Summary | Property | Description | | --- | --- | | Developer | inclusionAI | | Model type | Native audio-language Mixture-of-Experts model | | Parameters | 126B total parameters, 6.5B activated per inference step | | Inputs | Audio and text instructions | | Outputs | Text, or text with optional synthesized speech | | Primary languages | Chinese and English, including varied accents and dialects | | License | MIT | ## Highlights - **Complex speech recognition:** Handles Chinese and English speech, dialects, accents, noisy environments, and multi-speaker recordings. - **Long-audio understanding:** Comprehends and analyzes long-form recordings. - **Multidimensional perception:** Understands speech, non-speech sounds, acoustic scenes, and music. - **Audio reasoning:** Answers questions and performs reasoning over audio content. - **Audio interaction:** Produces text responses and can optionally synthesize speech with built-in voices or a reference voice. ## Architecture Ming-3.0-audio-flash combines an audio encoder and projector with a Mixture-of-Experts language backbone. An optional Talker generates speech responses from the model's output.

## Quick Start with Transformers The model uses custom Transformers code. Review the repository code before enabling `trust_remote_code=True`. ```bash git clone https://github.com/inclusionAI/Ming-3.0-audio-flash.git cd Ming-3.0-audio-flash python -m venv .venv-transformers source .venv-transformers/bin/activate pip install -r requirements-transformers.txt ``` ### Audio Understanding ```bash python examples/transformers_audio.py examples/audio/introduce_ant_group.wav \ --model inclusionAI/Ming-3.0-audio-flash \ --prompt "Please answer the question in the audio." ``` ### Speech Recognition ```bash python examples/transformers_audio.py examples/audio/introduce_ant_group.wav \ --model inclusionAI/Ming-3.0-audio-flash \ --task asr \ --max-new-tokens 256 \ --no-repeat-ngram-size 10 ``` The validated ASR prompt asks the model to identify the spoken language and place a tab between the language label and transcription. ### Direct Python Usage ```python import torch from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoProcessor model_id = "inclusionAI/Ming-3.0-audio-flash" audio_path = "examples/audio/introduce_ant_group.wav" processor = AutoProcessor.from_pretrained( model_id, trust_remote_code=True, use_fast=False, ) model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained( model_id, dtype=torch.bfloat16, device_map="auto", trust_remote_code=True, ).eval() messages = [ { "role": "user", "content": [ {"type": "audio", "audio": audio_path}, {"type": "text", "text": "Please answer the question in the audio."}, ], } ] inputs = processor(messages).to(model.device) inputs["audio_feats"] = inputs["audio_feats"].to(model.dtype) with torch.inference_mode(): output_ids = model.generate( **inputs, max_new_tokens=512, do_sample=False, ) generated_ids = output_ids[0, inputs["input_ids"].shape[1] :] response = processor.decode(generated_ids, skip_special_tokens=True).strip() print(response) ``` ## Speech Output The Talker example supports built-in voices and reference-audio voice prompting: ```bash python examples/transformers_thinker_talker.py \ --model inclusionAI/Ming-3.0-audio-flash \ --audio examples/audio/introduce_ant_group.wav \ --voice US_Stella \ --output output.wav ``` See the [voice guide](https://github.com/inclusionAI/Ming-3.0-audio-flash/blob/main/docs/voices.md) for available voice names and reference-audio usage. ## Serving ### vLLM-Omni ```bash export MODEL_PATH=inclusionAI/Ming-3.0-audio-flash MING_OUTPUT_MODE=text ./scripts/serve_vllm_omni.sh "$MODEL_PATH" ``` The reference 128K serving profile uses tensor parallelism across four 80 GB H800 GPUs. Select the deployment YAML that matches text-only or Talker output. On particularly long audio inputs, the four-GPU profiles may OOM; in that case, switch to the corresponding eight-GPU fallback profile (`deploy/*_8gpu.yaml`), which sets `tensor_parallel_size: 8` across GPUs 0–7 (and the Talker reuses GPU 7). See the [deployment guide](https://github.com/inclusionAI/Ming-3.0-audio-flash/blob/main/README.md#vllm-omni) for details. For speech output, start the audio profile and select an IP or registered voice with the vLLM-Omni client's `--voice` option: ```bash MING_OUTPUT_MODE=audio ./scripts/serve_vllm_omni.sh "$MODEL_PATH" python examples/vllm_omni_audio_chat.py examples/audio/introduce_ant_group.wav \ --audio-response \ --voice US_Stella \ --output-audio outputs/answer.wav ``` The client sends this selection as Chat Completions `audio.voice: {"id": "..."}`. vLLM-Omni uses the built-in IP voice `灵小柔` when no voice is specified. The model directory also provides `灵楷` and `US_James` as preset reference voices under `voice_presets/voice_audio/`, with their matching transcripts in `voice_presets/voice_prompts.json`. Both names are also available as built-in IP voices. ### SGLang ```bash export MODEL_PATH=inclusionAI/Ming-3.0-audio-flash ./scripts/serve_sglang.sh "$MODEL_PATH" ``` The validated SGLang profile uses four GPUs and provides text output. See the [SGLang example](https://github.com/inclusionAI/Ming-3.0-audio-flash/blob/main/examples/sglang_audio_chat.py) for client usage. ### SGLang-Omni [SGLang-Omni](https://sgl-project.github.io/sglang-omni/) serves transcription, audio chat, and speech synthesis from one server. Serving uses two GPUs: `--thinker.tp_size 2` places the thinker on both visible devices, the audio encoder uses GPU 0, and speech synthesis uses GPU 1. ```bash CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0,1 sgl-omni serve \ --model-path inclusionAI/Ming-3.0-audio-flash \ --thinker.tp_size 2 ``` The server exposes OpenAI-compatible `/v1/audio/transcriptions`, `/v1/audio/speech`, and `/v1/chat/completions` endpoints. See the [SGLang-Omni cookbook](https://sgl-project.github.io/sglang-omni/cookbook/ming3_audio.html) for client examples, including voice cloning with `ref_audio` and `ref_text`. ## Evaluation ### Speech Recognition

# RubatoCodec

[![Code: GitHub](https://img.shields.io/badge/Code-GitHub-black?logo=github)](https://github.com/third-intelligence/RubatoCodec)
[![Paper: arXiv](https://img.shields.io/badge/arXiv-2610.29434-b31b1b)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.29434)
[![License: Apache 2.0](https://img.shields.io/badge/License-Apache%202.0-blue)](https://www.apache.org/licenses/LICENSE-2.0)

RubatoCodec is a neural speech codec that divides speech into a fixed number of
variable-duration events. Each event carries discrete code indices and an
explicit duration. Event placement adapts to speech content, while the number of
events is determined exactly by the utterance length, so the token sequence
length a speech generator must produce is predictable. A causal decoder renders
completed events incrementally, which makes the codec suitable for streaming
text-to-speech.

The name comes from the musical term *rubato*: local timing flexes while the
overall tempo is preserved.

- **Adaptive Firing with an exact event budget.** Multi-scale latent
  dissimilarity and waveform spectral flux guide cumulative allocation on a
  50-Hz latent grid. For `T` frames the event count is exactly
  `max(1, min(T, round(0.25 · T)))`, giving 12.5 events/s. No learned boundary
  predictor, boundary labels, or rate loss is used.
- **Streaming decoding.** Events can be decoded one at a time or in chunks.
  Event-by-event decoding takes about 11 ms per event on an NVIDIA H200, well
  below the ~80 ms of audio each event represents on average.
- **Hybrid residual quantizer with depth control.** A semantically supervised
  FSQ first layer is followed by 15 DAC-style residual VQ layers, each with
  4,096 entries. Any prefix depth from 1 to 16 can be decoded, giving code-index
  bitrates of 0.15–2.4 kbit/s plus duration information.
- **Multilingual.** Trained on approximately 375,000 hours of speech, mostly
  English, Japanese, and Chinese, with 16-kHz input and 44.1-kHz output.

![RubatoCodec architecture](assets/architecture.png)

## Model details

| | |
|---|---|
| Input / output sample rate | 16 kHz / 44.1 kHz |
| Latent grid | 50 Hz |
| Event rate | 12.5 events/s (retention ratio 0.25) |
| Quantizer | 16 layers × 4,096 entries; layer 0 FSQ with semantic distillation, layers 1–15 residual VQ |
| Bitrate | 1.23 kbit/s at depth 8, 2.43 kbit/s at depth 16 (LibriSpeech, including duration information) |
| Decoder | Fully causal Transformer + ISTFT head, streaming capable |
| Parameters | 246M codec (72M encoder, 173M decoder, 1M quantizer) + frozen [w2v-BERT 2.0](https://huggingface.co/facebook/w2v-bert-2.0) (580M, encoding only) |
| License | Apache 2.0 |

## Usage

Install the package from the [GitHub repository](https://github.com/third-intelligence/RubatoCodec):

```bash
git clone https://github.com/third-intelligence/RubatoCodec
cd RubatoCodec
uv sync
```

Encode and decode:

```python
import soundfile as sf
import torch

from rubatocodec import RubatoCodec

codec = RubatoCodec.from_pretrained("third-intelligence/RubatoCodec", device="cuda")

data, sr = sf.read("speech.wav", dtype="float32")  # mono waveform
wav = torch.from_numpy(data)

enc = codec.encode(wav, sr=sr)       # {"codes": (16, K) int64, "durs": (K,) int64}
audio = codec.decode(enc)            # (1, 1, T_audio) at 44.1 kHz, full depth
audio = codec.decode(enc, depth=8)   # lower bitrate with the first 8 layers

sf.write("recon.wav", audio[0, 0].cpu().numpy(), codec.output_sr)
```

`durs` gives each event's duration in 20-ms grid frames. Loading also downloads
`facebook/w2v-bert-2.0`, which is used only for encoding.

Streaming decoding, inference settings, the code format, and training are
documented in the repository:
[inference guide](https://github.com/third-intelligence/RubatoCodec/blob/main/docs/inference.md),
[architecture](https://github.com/third-intelligence/RubatoCodec/blob/main/docs/architecture.md),
[training](https://github.com/third-intelligence/RubatoCodec/blob/main/docs/training.md).

## Evaluation

RubatoCodec is evaluated on LibriSpeech test-clean, VCTK, JVS nonpara30, JVNV,
and seed-tts-eval test-zh against 13 other codecs. At comparable bitrates, it
shows the best intelligibility preservation among the compared codecs on the
English and Japanese benchmarks and high predicted quality, while the strongest
comparators achieve higher PESQ-WB and STOI.

dWER/dCER compare ASR transcripts of the reconstructed and original audio

# KittenTTS 2

A 1.7B speech language model with in-context voice cloning. It reads text and writes S3
codec tokens, which a vocoder turns into 24 kHz audio.

```bash
pip install kittenml
```

```python
from kittenml import KittenTTS
import soundfile as sf

m = KittenTTS("KittenML/kitten-tts-2")

# a built-in voice
audio = m.generate("Hi! umm.. how are you, I guess?  .. uh.. nice to meet you??",
                   voice="WeatherPresenterCheerful")

# or clone one, from 5-30 seconds of a single speaker
audio = m.generate("This is my own voice.", reference="my_voice.wav")

sf.write("output.wav", audio, m.sample_rate)
```

Everything the model needs is in this repository, so no Hugging Face login is required.

## Voices

`m.available_voices` lists all 115. Bella, Jasper, Luna, Bruno, Rosie, Hugo, Kiki
and Leo are the same speakers as in KittenTTS 0.8, so existing code keeps working.

Voices named after a person are English. The rest are named for the language they
speak followed by what they are — `SpanishAbuela`, `JapaneseTrainConductor`,
`RussianBabushka` — and are how you reach those languages, since the voice is what
carries the accent. Nine older entries carry a bare language name: Arabic, Chinese,
French, German, Hindi, Italian, Portuguese, Russian, Spanish.

```python
m.generate("Guten Morgen. Ich wünsche dir einen wunderschönen Tag.",
           voice="German", normalize=False)

m.generate("Buenas tardes. Hoy vamos a preparar algo muy especial.",
           voice="SpanishAbuela", normalize=False)
```

Sixteen languages have a named voice: Arabic, Chinese, Dutch, French, German, Hindi,
Indonesian, Italian, Japanese, Korean, Polish, Portuguese, Russian, Spanish, Turkish,
and English.

Pass `normalize=False` for non-English text: the text normalizer is English-tuned and
will mangle numbers and dates in other languages.

## Expression controls

> **Beta.** Emotion control steers delivery rather than guaranteeing it, and the effect
> varies by voice and by sentence.

```python
m.generate("[joyful] We won the grant <laugh> I can (((hardly))) believe it!",
           voice="Kiki", preset="expressive")
```

A leading `[emotion]` tag, inline `<event>` tags and `(((emphasis)))` spans reach the
model as markup rather than being spoken, and switch on its expression conditioning.

**Emotions** — one leading tag sets the emotion for the whole line:

`[angry]` `[contemplative]` `[excited]` `[joyful]` `[mundane]`
`[nervous]` `[sad]` `[stern]` `[surprised]` `[tender]`

**Vocal events** — inline, anywhere in the line:

`<gasp>` `<giggle>` `<growl>` `<gulp>` `<laugh>`
`<pause>` `<scoff>` `<sigh>` `<sob>` `<um>`

**Emphasis** — triple parentheses stress a word or short phrase:

```python
m.generate("I told you (((never))) to open that door.", voice="Victor")
```

Only these twenty tags are recognised. They are the most common of the many in the
training data, so a rarer one such as `[reverent]` is spoken as ordinary text rather
than treated as markup — as is anything else bracketed, like `section [3]` or `x < 5`.

## Weight variants

The language model ships in three packings of the same weights. `weights=` picks one;
`model.available_weights` lists them.

| `weights=` | On disk | |
|---|---|---|
| `"packed"` *(default)* | 954 MB | 1.58-bit ternary body, bf16 embedding. **Lossless** |
| `"emb4"` | 469 MB | Same body in TL2, plus a 4-bit embedding. **Lossy** |
| `"full"` | 3469 MB | Plain bf16 |

```python
m = KittenTTS("KittenML/kitten-tts-2", weights="emb4")
```

Only the variant you ask for is downloaded.

`emb4` halves the download, and the saving is almost entirely the token embedding — 324M
parameters that `packed` has to leave at bf16 because they are not ternary. Its transformer
body is still bit-exact: all 313 non-embedding tensors reproduce `full` exactly. The
embedding is not, at L2 relative error 0.118 against the bf16 export, and it is coded at
4.21 bits per weight across three frequency tiers. That is the one lossy thing here, which
is why `packed` stays the default.

## Decoders

Audio is decoded in two stages, and the first can be swapped for a smaller distilled
student with weights packed to 4 or 8 bits:

```python
m = KittenTTS("KittenML/kitten-tts-2", decoder="student_w4")
```

| Decoder | Flow on disk | |
|---|---|---|
| `default` | 459 MB | Best quality |
| `student_w4` | 39 MB | Distilled single-step student, weights packed to 4 bits |

These trade fidelity for footprint, not for speed: quantisation shrinks storage and
memory bandwidth, not arithmetic.

## What is in here

```
lm/          the speech language model, plus its spk_proj speaker head
speaker/     the speaker-embedding model used when cloning
voices/      reference clips, transcripts, and precomputed embeddings
decoders/    the optional 4-bit decoder
cpp/         GGUF weights for the llama.cpp fork, see "Running on CPU"
config.json  token layout, decode presets, voice and decoder indexes
```

The weights are 947 MiB: 910 MiB for the language model and 37 MiB for the decoder.
A load pulls those rather than the whole repository, and only the decoder you ask for.

The language model's linear weights are ternary — within every 128-wide group each
value is exactly one of `{-scale, 0, +scale}` — so bf16 spends 16 bits to say one of
three things. `lm/model-ternary.safetensors` packs them five trits to a byte, 1.6 bits
per weight, with each group keeping its scale at full precision:

| | |
|---|---|
| `lm/model.safetensors` | 3.47 GB, bf16 throughout |
| `lm/model-ternary.safetensors` | **0.95 GB**, the same weights, 3.6x smaller |

The packing is exact rather than approximate, so the two produce bit-identical audio.
`config.json` points `lm_packed` at the smaller file and that is what gets downloaded;
the full file stays for anything loading this with plain `transformers`.

## Running on CPU

KittenTTS 2 runs on CPU out of the box — `device` is auto-detected — but the fastest way
is [kitten-tts-2-cpp](https://github.com/KittenML/kitten-tts-2-cpp), our llama.cpp fork.
The `cpp/` directory here holds what it needs: the GGUF language model and its decoders.

## Requirements

Python 3.10 or later, and PyTorch.

speaker-embedding model, under [MIT](speaker/LICENSE), and the `kittenml` Python package that
loads this repository, under Apache 2.0.

# SteerTTS v1

A small English text-to-speech model that you steer with numbers. Each request can set any subset of **12 acoustic
controls**, for example speaking rate, loudness, median pitch, pitch range, final rise or fall, pauses, spectral tilt
and breathiness. Each control is a z-score relative to the chosen voice's own neutral speech. You can also pick a
**style tag**, give a **free-text direction** (which a small adapter turns into a request you can inspect), or use
**inline markup**. The model can **clone** a voice from a short reference clip.

| | |
|---|---|
| Acoustic model | **9.59M** parameters (encoder/decoder: attention + bidirectional Mamba-3, AdaLN conditioning) |
| + Vocos vocoder | 13.53M (`charactr/vocos-mel-24khz`, frozen), **23.1M** total |
| Flow-matching refiner (optional, on by default) | 17.64M → 40.8M total |
| Prompted flow (cloning only) | 24.67M, used in place of the refiner when `ref_wav` is given → 47.8M total |
| Frozen external encoders | WavLM-base-plus-sv 101M (cloning only), all-MiniLM-L6-v2 22.7M (free-text prompts only) |
| Output | 24 kHz mono, fp32, CPU or CUDA |
| Voices | 2,825 built-in voices under anonymised names (`voice_0001` …), default `voice_1688` (v1.0.0: `voice_1361`) |

> **Licence: weights CC BY-NC 4.0 (non-commercial use only); package code MIT.** The weights were trained partly on
> non-commercial data (see [Training data](#training-data)).

I can help you reschedule your appointment today." | <audio controls preload="none" src="https://huggingface.co/WhissleAI/steer-tts/resolve/main/samples/cmp_intro_voice_1361.mp3"></audio> | <audio controls preload="none" src="https://huggingface.co/WhissleAI/steer-tts/resolve/main/samples/cmp_intro_voice_1688.mp3"></audio> |

| Same text, `ctrl={"f0_end": 2, "f0_iqr": 1.5}`: rising, livelier | <audio controls preload="none" src="https://huggingface.co/WhissleAI/steer-tts/resolve/main/samples/steer_question_rise.mp3"></audio> |

## Quick start

```bash
git clone https://huggingface.co/WhissleAI/steer-tts && cd steer-tts      # or huggingface_hub.snapshot_download("WhissleAI/steer-tts")
pip install ".[all]"          # core: torch, vocos, g2p_en …; [all] adds transformers (prompts, cloning), parselmouth (measuring), sounddevice (playback)
# or, code only (weights download on first use): pip install "steertts[all] @ git+https://github.com/WhissleAI/steer-tts"
steertts say "Hello there, nice to meet you." -o hello.wav
steertts say "I can't believe it worked." --tag happiness --ctrl rate=1,f0_iqr=1.5 -o happy.wav
steertts say "Please keep this quiet." --prompt "whispering, slow and secretive" -o secret.wav   # prints the resolved request
steertts stream "Well, *that* was fast. [pause 400ms] <slow>Let me think.</slow>" -o markup.wav
steertts play "Hi there. <whisper>This plays as it is rendered.</whisper>"       # streams to your speakers
steertts say "Now in your voice." --ref-wav consenting_speaker.wav -o clone.wav
steertts voices --gender female | head
steertts --precision int8 say "Same voice, a quarter of the download." -o int8.wav   # int8 weights (see Quantized int8)
```

The CLI looks for the model in the current directory. From anywhere else, pass it before the command
(`steertts --model WhissleAI/steer-tts say "Hi." -o hi.wav`) or set `STEERTTS_MODEL`.

```python
from steertts import SteerTTS

tts = SteerTTS.from_pretrained("WhissleAI/steer-tts")   # HF repo id or a local dir; device: cuda if available, else cpu
wav = tts("The meeting moved to Thursday.")       # float32 numpy, 24 kHz, default voice voice_1688
wav = tts("Are you serious?", voice="voice_0042", ctrl={"f0_end": 2.0, "f0_iqr": 1.5})   # rising, lively
wav = tts("It is over.", tag="sadness", ctrl={"loud": -1}, guidance=1.5)

req = tts.resolve({"text": "See you soon.", "prompt": "excited, a bit faster"})
print(req)    # {'text': ..., 'voice': 'voice_1688', 'tag': 'excited', 'ctrl': {'rate': 0.29}, 'prompt_mapping': {...}, ...}
wav = tts.synthesize(req)                         # a resolved request renders exactly as the prompt would

from steertts.player import Player                 # plays chunks as they arrive (sounddevice, else ffplay / aplay)
player = Player(tts.sample_rate)
for chunk in tts.stream("First sentence. Second sentence."):   # sentence-level streaming
    player.play(chunk.audio)
player.close()                                                 # waits until playback finishes
tts.save(wav, "out.wav")

tts8 = SteerTTS.from_pretrained("WhissleAI/steer-tts", precision="int8")   # downloads only int8/ (52 MB, not 215 MB)
```

`inference.py` renders one example of each feature. `python -m steertts.cli --help` lists the CLI.

## The request

Every synthesis is one JSON object. It is documented field by field in [`request.schema.json`](request.schema.json)
(JSON Schema 2020-12; `steertts schema` prints it). Only `text` is required.

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `text` | English text. Numbers, units, currency, ordinals, ranges and unknown acronyms are spelled out. |
| `voice` / `ref_wav` | A built-in voice, **or** a reference clip to clone (first 8 s, at least 0.5 s). |
| `tag` | One of 51 style tags (`none`, `whisper`, `sadness`, `anger`, `fast`, `high_pitch`, …). |
| `ctrl` | `{control: z}` over the 12 controls below, each in [-5, 5]. |
| `prompt` | Free-text direction. `resolve()` maps it to `tag` + `ctrl`; an explicit `tag` or `ctrl` dim wins. |
| `guidance` | Steering scale s (default 1). See [Guidance](#how-well-it-steers). |
| `pace` | Global tempo divisor (>1 is faster). It does not change the style. |
| `word_shift` | `{word_index: {pitch: st, energy: dB, dur: ×}}`, per-word prosody edits. Not with `markup` or `stream()` (they raise an error); use inline markup there. |
| `markup` | Parse inline markup in `text` (see below). `stream()` always parses it. |
| `flow`, `seed` | Use the flow refiner (default true) and set the sampler seed. Renders are deterministic per device. |

**Controls and the mask.** The 12 controls are utterance-level acoustic measurements:

- `rate`: articulation rate
- `loud`: speech level
- `f0_med`: median pitch
- `f0_iqr`: pitch range
- `f0_end`: final pitch slope
- `pause`: pause share
- `tilt`: spectral tilt
- `voiced`: voiced share
- `flat`: spectral flatness
- `centroid`: spectral centroid
- `cpps`: cepstral peak prominence
- `h1h2`: H1–H2

Each value is a z-score against the chosen voice's own neutral speech, in units of the pooled within-speaker SD
(`control_stats.json`). The model also receives an availability mask:

- A dim named in `ctrl` is requested.
- A dim left out is unspecified, and the model chooses it from voice, tag and text.
- `{"rate": 0}` asks for this voice's neutral rate. Omitting `rate` lets a `fast` tag or the text decide.

`steertts measure out.wav --text "…" --voice voice_1688` reads the controls back with the same measurement code
that labelled the training data.

**Markup** (`markup: true` or `stream()`):

| Markup | Effect |
|---|---|
| `*word*` or `<emph>…</emph>` | Emphasis: +2.5 st, +4 dB, ×1.2 duration |
| `<slow> <fast> <high> <low> <loud> <soft>` | Per-word changes; the sentence is still rendered in one pass |
| `[pause]`, `[pause 300ms]`, `[pause 1.5s]` | Exact silence |
| `<whisper>…</whisper>` (any tag), `<style prompt="…">…</style>` | The span is rendered as its own segment |

Text is rendered sentence by sentence, so the first sentence can play while the rest renders.

## Architecture

FastPitch-style explicit-variance TTS:

1. **Front end.** g2p_en ARPAbet phonemes with word indices.
2. **Encoder.** 4 blocks.
3. **Variance predictors.** Per-phone duration, pitch and energy.
4. **Length regulator.**
5. **Decoder.** 4 blocks.
6. **Output.** A 100-band log-mel, rendered by Vocos.

Each encoder/decoder block is a **hybrid**: multi-head self-attention, then a **bidirectional Mamba-3** branch (two
Mamba-3 layers run forward and backward and summed; complex-valued state, trapezoidal discretisation; 3.70M
parameters in total), then a conv FFN.

Every LayerNorm in every block and predictor is an **adaptive LayerNorm**. Its scale and shift are predicted from
g = MLP([speaker vector, tag embedding, ctrl ⊙ mask, mask]). The speaker slot is a linear projection of a frozen
512-d WavLM-base-plus-sv x-vector. Built-in voices use their stored mean vector; cloning uses the vector of the
reference clip.

**Guidance** renders the request and the uninstructed request, then extrapolates durations, pitch, energy and mel:
out = out₀ + s·(out − out₀).

Optional decoders:

- **Flow refiner.** A conditional flow-matching ConvNeXt network (OT-CFM, 10 midpoint steps, temperature 0.4). It
  samples mel detail given the acoustic model's mel and g, so every control still comes from the acoustic model.
- **Prompted flow.** The same network plus attention, given the reference clip's own mel as context
  (Voicebox-style infilling). Used for cloning.

The `steertts` package here is self-contained. It is the inference subset of the training code, operation for
operation, and its outputs are bit-identical to the training repository's synthesis on the same device (see
[Release verification](#release-verification)).

## How well it steers

The numbers below are **held-out**: 16 LibriTTS-R test-clean speakers who share no speaker, chapter or recording
with the training data (8 female, 8 male by a median-F0 rule; the corpus has no gender labels on disk), each
conditioned on the speaker vector of one recording, × 8 texts. They are for the acoustic model at guidance 1 **without the flow refiner**.
Steering through the refiner was not measured in the paper; the release check below confirms only the direction.

Columns:

- **Hit**: share of renders that move more than 0.5 SD the requested way.
- **Δz**: achieved change for a request of ±2.
- **ρ**: Spearman correlation between request and readback (by our extractor / by Praat).

| Tier | Control | Hit at −2 / +2 | Δz at −2 / +2 | ρ (ours / Praat) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Reliable** | loud | 1.00 / 1.00 | −1.57 / +1.81 | .97 / .97 |
| | f0_med | .98 / 1.00 | −1.15 / +1.18 | .95 / .95 |
| | h1h2 | 1.00 / 1.00 | −1.59 / +1.49 | .96 / .96 |
| | tilt | 1.00 / .99 | −1.39 / +0.97 | .96 / .87 |
| | centroid | .78 / .94 | −0.79 / +1.20 | .92 / .92 |
| | f0_iqr | .66 / .91 | −0.63 / +1.09 | .88 / .88 |
| **Usable** | rate | 1.00 / 1.00 | −1.61 / +1.30 | .96 / .66 |
| | f0_end | .96 / .99 | −0.85 / +1.31 | .94 / .83 |
| | flat | .62 / .41 | −0.64 / +0.51 | .85 / .68 |
| **Weak** | pause | .38 / .64 | −0.37 / +0.71 | .76 / .70 |
| | voiced | .39 / .12 | −0.44 / +0.26 | .79 / .60 |
| | cpps | .56 / .35 | −0.45 / +0.30 | .58 / .46 |

**Larger re-measurement** (same model, protocol and extractor; 62 unseen voices: 31 LibriTTS-R test-clean + 31 GLOBE
test, a corpus the model never trained on; × 16 sentences, 12 of them newly written; 992 renders per direction per
control; 95% CI from a crossed voice × sentence bootstrap):

| Control | Hit at −2 / +2 | Mean hit [95% CI] | Δz at −2 / +2 |
|---|---|---|---|
| loud | 1.00 / 1.00 | 1.00 [1.00, 1.00] | −1.54 / +1.87 |
| rate | 1.00 / 1.00 | 1.00 [1.00, 1.00] | −1.52 / +1.27 |
| h1h2 | 1.00 / 1.00 | 1.00 [1.00, 1.00] | −1.63 / +1.53 |
| tilt | 1.00 / .98 | .99 [.98, 1.00] | −1.42 / +0.93 |
| f0_med | 1.00 / .99 | .99 [.98, 1.00] | −1.21 / +1.31 |
| centroid | .90 / .96 | .93 [.83, 1.00] | −0.93 / +1.37 |
| f0_end | .85 / .93 | .89 [.81, .95] | −0.81 / +1.11 |
| f0_iqr | .59 / .88 | .73 [.63, .83] | −0.58 / +0.95 |

LibriTTS-R and GLOBE voices are statistically indistinguishable. `f0_end` depends on the sentence more than the other
controls do.

- **Tiers.** Reliable: ρ ≥ 0.85 under both extractors. Usable: under one. Weak: under neither.
- **Gain.** The mean gain (achieved / requested) is about 0.5. `rate` and `f0_med` at +1 hit only .48 / .42.
- **Cross-talk.** Mean leakage into the other 11 dims is 0.15–0.30 SD. The off-diagonal / diagonal ratio is 0.10.
- **CPPS** is not a working control: a request moves pitch and level about as much as CPPS itself.
- **Intelligibility.** WER (Whisper-large-v3) is 0.94 % uninstructed and 0.84–1.01 % across all requests.

**Guidance** (pooled over loud, rate, f0_med, f0_iqr and tilt; ±2 requests; n = 1,280):

| s | Steer ratio (Δz / requested) | Hit | Leak | WER |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 0.65 | .95 | .20 | 0.9 % |
| 2 | 1.35 | .99 | .34 | 1.0 % |
| 3 | 1.97 | .98 | .48 | 1.0 % |

- s ≈ 1.5 roughly delivers the requested size, at the cost of more leakage.
- Guidance on tags is riskier: `whisper` at s = 3 raises WER to 16 %.

**Markup** (8 held-out voices × 6 sentences × 2 words):

- Emphasis achieved +2.58 st and +3.92 dB, against +2.5 st and +4 dB requested.
- `<high>` / `<low>` gave +3.18 / −2.96 st for ±3.
- `<loud>` / `<soft>` gave +4.84 / −5.54 dB for ±6. The decoder attenuates level by 10–20 %.
- `<slow>` / `<fast>` and pauses are exact by construction.
- Neighbouring words move by at most 0.19 st and 0.16 dB.

**Free-text prompts** (161 hand-written prompts):

- Which-dims precision / recall: .85 / .66. Sign accuracy: .88.
- Tag top-1 / top-3: .56 / .69.
- Composition (.23) and negation (.22) mostly fail. "Not fast" can come out fast.
- Absolute-register prompts ("a deep male voice") are not supported. Pick a voice instead (`voices.json`).
- **Always look at the resolved request.**

## Quality

Results under the Open TTS Leaderboard protocol (run locally on an RTX 5070, not an official submission;
Qwen3-ASR-1.7B WER, WavLM-large SIM):

| Setting | Seed-TTS en | CV3-Eval en | Avg |
|---|---|---|---|
| `voice_1361` (v1.0.0 default), acoustic model + Vocos, WER | 1.00 % | 2.63 % | **1.81 %** |
| Cloning (prompted flow), WER / SIM ×100 | 1.01 % / 37.4 | 2.73 % / 28.7 | 1.87 % / 33.1 |

- The flow refiner was scored with an earlier acoustic checkpoint: 1.04 % / 2.70 % WER (no change).
- **Cloning similarity is low.** The board's lowest cloning SIM is about 37, and its median is about 65. Do not

## Quantized int8

`precision="int8"` (CLI `--precision int8`) loads the weight files in `int8/` and downloads only those: 52 MB instead
of 215 MB. Vocos, WavLM-base-plus-sv and all-MiniLM-L6-v2 still come from their own repos and are rounded to int8 the
same way when they load. The whole install shrinks from 765 MB to 193 MB of weights, and RAM use does not change.

- **Scheme.** Weight-only, round-to-nearest, symmetric. Tensors with ≥ 2 dimensions and ≥ 1,024 values are stored as
  int8 with one fp16 scale per output row; everything else as fp16. Weights are dequantized at load and compute stays
  fp32, so int8 is not faster than fp32. `steertts/quant.py` has the code.
- **Parity.** The package's int8 renders are bit-identical to the evaluated int8 model on plain, control, prompt, markup
  and cloning requests.

Same protocol and machine as [Quality](#quality), default voice `voice_1361`, refiner on:

| | fp32 | int8 |
|---|---|---|
| Seed-TTS en WER | 0.94 % | 1.03 % |
| CV3-Eval en WER | 2.62 % | 2.66 % |
| Cloning WER, Seed / CV3 | 0.99 % / 2.70 % | 1.06 % / 2.70 % |
| Cloning SIM ×100, Seed / CV3 | 37.4 / 28.7 | 37.5 / 28.3 |
| UTMOS22, Seed / CV3 | 4.27 / 4.24 | 4.27 / 4.25 |
| UTMOS22 cloning, Seed / CV3 | 4.15 / 4.08 | 4.13 / 4.07 |

Steering readback (8 voices × 6 texts, request −2 / +2, achieved Δz):

| control | fp32 | int8 |
|---|---|---|
| loud | −1.73 / +1.92 | −1.71 / +1.91 |
| f0_med | −1.02 / +1.39 | −1.01 / +1.50 |
| rate | −1.55 / +1.29 | −1.54 / +1.33 |
| h1h2 | −1.07 / +1.21 | −1.05 / +1.14 |
| tilt | −1.28 / +0.86 | −1.31 / +0.92 |
| f0_iqr | −0.58 / +0.80 | −0.67 / +0.75 |

- **Free-text prompts.** Of the 161 hand-written prompts, 97 % map to the same tag and 96 % to the same set of
  controls as fp32.
- **Not released: int4.** Uniform int4 (7× smaller) loses about 0.5 UTMOS and 5–7 cloning SIM points, and pitch-range
  steering falls to ±0.3. Keeping the conditioning path in int8 recovers the steering but not the audio quality.

## Speed

Measured on an RTX 5070 and on a shared, heavily loaded 8-thread CPU, so treat CPU figures as lower bounds:

- **GPU.** Batch-1 RTFx 61–81 for the acoustic model + Vocos (leaderboard runs).
- **CPU, 8 threads.** RTFx 3.6–7.9 for the acoustic model + Vocos. The flow refiner adds 12× the compute and
  drops RTFx from 6.7 to 0.8 (0.4 with 1 thread). Use `flow=False` / `--no-flow` for real-time CPU use.
- **Cloning on CPU.** RTFx 0.2 with the prompted flow, including the WavLM speaker encoder.
- **Streaming on CPU.** First audio after about 1 s.
- See [Release verification](#release-verification) for the numbers measured on this exact package.

## Limitations

- **English only.** The front end is ARPAbet. Single speaker per request, and the controls are utterance-level.
- **Emotion tags are style switches, not emotions.** An independent emotion classifier (emotion2vec+ large)
  recognises only `sadness` (0.16 top-1 vs 0.01 uninstructed). Every other emotion tag scores at most 0.02. The same
  classifier recognises 7 of 10 of these emotions on real EARS recordings. 27 of 49 tags are acoustically within 0.5
  of `neutral`. Voice-quality tags such as `whisper` act strongly (voiced share −9.9 SD).
- **Event tokens only reserve time.** `[laugh]`, `[cough]`, `[dog]`, … add about 0.12 s of near-silence. An audio
  tagger detects 0 of 1,728 renders. The project's demo mixed recorded sounds in, but that mixer is not part of this
  release.
- **The acoustic-environment input is untrained.** The weights contain an environment projection, but the final
  training stage never saw a non-zero environment vector, so this package does not expose it.
- **Cloning similarity is low** (see above), and cloning speed on CPU is slow with the prompted flow.
- **The controls are acoustic measurements, not percepts.** `voiced`, `flat` and `cpps` barely move. `rate` and
  `tilt` depend on how they are measured. z = 0 is the voice's typical render, not its real recordings.
- **Test-set-informed choices.** The prompted-flow checkpoint was chosen on subsets of the Seed-TTS / CV3 test
  sets, and the text-normalisation rules came from CV3 error analysis. The leaderboard rows use `voice_1361`,
  the pre-registered v1.0.0 default: a sweep picked a lower-WER voice on the test sets, but it was not used.
  v1.0.1 switched the package default to `voice_1688` after users found `voice_1361` fast and synthetic-sounding.
  It was picked by UTMOS22 over 300 random voices on our own sentences, not on the test sets. On 16 sentences it
  matches `voice_1361` on WER (1.1 %), scores higher on UTMOS22 (4.43 vs 4.24) and speaks a little slower (3.4 vs 3.6
  words/s). Pass `voice="voice_1361"` for the v1.0.0 sound.
- **No human evaluation.** Every number above is from automatic metrics, with one training seed.

## Intended use and misuse

**Intended uses:**

- Research on controllable / interpretable speech synthesis.
- Accessibility and prototyping, where explicit, inspectable control matters more than peak naturalness.
- On-device experiments with a ~23M-parameter TTS.

**Voice cloning requires consent.** Clone only a voice whose owner has agreed, and do not use this model to:

- impersonate real people;
- produce deceptive or fraudulent audio;
- bypass voice authentication;
- create non-consensual content.

Disclose synthetic speech to listeners. There is no watermark yet.

**Built-in voices are anonymised.** Built-in voices are training speakers under opaque names. Speaker IDs from the
source corpora are not included. Speakers from a celebrity-interview corpus (VoxCeleb, via NonverbalTTS) were
excluded from the voice list.

## Release verification

The package was verified in a fresh CPU environment; `TEST_LOG.md` has the full log.

- **Tests.** The pytest suite passes (16 tests at v1.0.0; 17 at v1.0.1, re-run with the new default voice; 21 at
  v1.1.0, with the int8 tests).
- **Parity.** Seven renders are bit-identical to the training code's synthesis on the same device: acoustic
  only, controls, tag + guidance, per-word shifts, the flow refiner, and cloning through the prompted flow.
- **Speed.** On this package, CPU with 4 threads on a loaded machine: RTFx 4.9 without the refiner, 0.7 with it.

## 📖 Model Introduction GLM-TTS is a high-quality text-to-speech (TTS) synthesis system based on large language models, supporting zero-shot voice cloning and streaming inference. The system adopts a two-stage architecture combining an LLM for speech token generation and a Flow Matching model for waveform synthesis. By introducing a **Multi-Reward Reinforcement Learning** framework, GLM-TTS significantly improves the expressiveness of generated speech, achieving more natural emotional control compared to traditional TTS systems. ### Key Features * **Zero-shot Voice Cloning:** Clone any speaker's voice with just 3-10 seconds of prompt audio. * **RL-enhanced Emotion Control:** Utilizes a multi-reward reinforcement learning framework (GRPO) to optimize prosody and emotion. * **High-quality Synthesis:** Generates speech comparable to commercial systems with reduced Character Error Rate (CER). * **Phoneme-level Control:** Supports "Hybrid Phoneme + Text" input for precise pronunciation control (e.g., polyphones). * **Streaming Inference:** Supports real-time audio generation suitable for interactive applications. * **Bilingual Support:** Optimized for Chinese and English mixed text. ## System Architecture GLM-TTS follows a two-stage design: 1. **Stage 1 (LLM):** A Llama-based model converts input text into speech token sequences. 2. **Stage 2 (Flow Matching):** A Flow model converts token sequences into high-quality mel-spectrograms, which are then turned into waveforms by a vocoder.
### Reinforcement Learning Alignment To tackle flat emotional expression, GLM-TTS uses a **Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO)** algorithm with multiple reward functions (Similarity, CER, Emotion, Laughter) to align the LLM's generation strategy. ## Evaluation Results Evaluated on `seed-tts-eval`. **GLM-TTS_RL** achieves the lowest Character Error Rate (CER) while maintaining high speaker similarity. | Model | CER ↓ | SIM ↑ | Open-source | | :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | | Seed-TTS | 1.12 | **79.6** | 🔒 No | | CosyVoice2 | 1.38 | 75.7 | 👐 Yes | | F5-TTS | 1.53 | 76.0 | 👐 Yes | | **GLM-TTS (Base)** | 1.03 | 76.1 | 👐 Yes | | **GLM-TTS_RL (Ours)** | **0.89** | 76.4 | 👐 Yes | ## Quick Start ### Installation ```bash git clone [https://github.com/zai-org/GLM-TTS.git](https://github.com/zai-org/GLM-TTS.git) cd GLM-TTS pip install -r requirements.txt ``` #### Command Line Inference ```bash python glmtts_inference.py \ --data=example_zh \ --exp_name=_test \ --use_cache \ # --phoneme # Add this flag to enable phoneme capabilities. ``` #### Shell Script Inference ```bash bash glmtts_inference.sh ``` ## Acknowledgments & Citation We thank the following open-source projects for their support: - [CosyVoice](https://github.com/FunAudioLLM/CosyVoice) - Providing frontend processing framework and high-quality vocoder - [Llama](https://github.com/meta-llama/llama) - Providing basic language model architecture - [Vocos](https://github.com/charactr-platform/vocos) - Providing high-quality vocoder - [GRPO-Zero](https://github.com/policy-gradient/GRPO-Zero) - Reinforcement learning algorithm implementation inspiration If you find GLM-TTS useful for your research, please cite our technical report: ```bibtex @misc{cui2025glmttstechnicalreport, title={GLM-TTS Technical Report}, author={Jiayan Cui and Zhihan Yang and Naihan Li and Jiankun Tian and Xingyu Ma and Yi Zhang and Guangyu Chen and Runxuan Yang and Yuqing Cheng and Yizhi Zhou and Guochen Yu and Xiaotao Gu and Jie Tang}, year={2025}, eprint={2512.14291}, archivePrefix={arXiv}, primaryClass={cs.SD}, url={https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.14291}, } }

models.card_text: --- language: - zh - en - ar - my - da - nl - fi - fr - de - el - he - hi - id - it - ja - km - ko - lo - ms - no - pl - pt - ru - es - sw - sv - tl - th - tr - vi license: apache-2.0 library_name: voxcpm tags: - text-to-speech - tts - multilingual - voice-cloning - voice-design - diffusion - audio pipeline_tag: text-to-speech --- # VoxCPM2 **VoxCPM2** is a tokenizer-free, diffusion autoregressive Text-to-Speech model — **2B parameters**, **30 languages**, **48kHz** audio output, trained on over **2 million hours** of multilingual speech data. [![GitHub](https://img.shields.io/badge/GitHub-VoxCPM-blue?logo=github)](https://github.com/OpenBMB/VoxCPM) [![Docs](https://img.shields.io/badge/Docs-ReadTheDocs-8CA1AF)](https://voxcpm.readthedocs.io/en/latest/) [![Demo](https://img.shields.io/badge/Live%20Playground-Demo-orange)](https://huggingface.co/spaces/OpenBMB/VoxCPM-Demo) [![Audio Samples](https://img.shields.io/badge/Audio%20Samples-Demo%20Page-green)](https://openbmb.github.io/voxcpm2-demopage) [![Discord](https://img.shields.io/badge/Discord-VoxCPM-5865F2?logo=discord&logoColor=white)](https://discord.gg/KZUx7tVNwz) [![Lark](https://img.shields.io/badge/飞书群-VoxCPM-00D6B9?logo=lark&logoColor=white)](https://applink.feishu.cn/client/chat/chatter/add_by_link?link_token=acds0b9d-23d8-4d7e-b696-d200f3e22a7f) [![MiniCPM Wiki](https://img.shields.io/badge/MiniCPM-Wiki-1677FF?logo=readthedocs&logoColor=white)](https://modelbest.feishu.cn/wiki/UtWxwcERfiRIpIkBOjuc3h9tn1D) ## Highlights - 🌍 **30-Language Multilingual** — No language tag needed; input text in any supported language directly - 🎨 **Voice Design** — Generate a novel voice from a natural-language description alone (gender, age, tone, emotion, pace…); no reference audio required - 🎛️ **Controllable Cloning** — Clone any voice from a short clip, with optional style guidance to steer emotion, pace, and expression while preserving timbre - 🎙️ **Ultimate Cloning** — Provide reference audio + its transcript for audio-continuation cloning; every vocal nuance faithfully reproduced - 🔊 **48kHz Studio-Quality Output** — Accepts 16kHz reference; outputs 48kHz via AudioVAE V2's built-in super-resolution, no external upsampler needed - 🧠 **Context-Aware Synthesis** — Automatically infers appropriate prosody and expressiveness from text content - ⚡ **Real-Time Streaming** — RTF as low as ~0.3 on NVIDIA RTX 4090, and ~0.13 accelerated by [Nano-VLLM](https://github.com/a710128/nanovllm-voxcpm) - 📜 **Fully Open-Source & Commercial-Ready** — Apache-2.0 license, free for commercial use Supported Languages (30) Arabic, Burmese, Chinese, Danish, Dutch, English, Finnish, French, German, Greek, Hebrew, Hindi, Indonesian, Italian, Japanese, Khmer, Korean, Lao, Malay, Norwegian, Polish, Portuguese, Russian, Spanish, Swahili, Swedish, Tagalog, Thai, Turkish, Vietnamese Chinese Dialects: 四川话, 粤语, 吴语, 东北话, 河南话, 陕西话, 山东话, 天津话, 闽南话 ## Quick Start ### Installation ```bash pip install voxcpm ``` **Requirements:** Python ≥ 3.10, PyTorch ≥ 2.5.0, CUDA ≥ 12.0 · [Full Quick Start →](https://voxcpm.readthedocs.io/en/latest/quickstart.html) ### Text-to-Speech ```python from voxcpm import VoxCPM import soundfile as sf model = VoxCPM.from_pretrained("openbmb/VoxCPM2", load_denoiser=False) wav = model.generate( text="VoxCPM2 brings multilingual support, creative voice design, and controllable voice cloning.", cfg_value=2.0, inference_timesteps=10, ) sf.write("output.wav", wav, model.tts_model.sample_rate) ``` ### Voice Design Put the voice description in parentheses at the start of `text`, followed by the content to synthesize: ```python wav = model.generate( text="(A young woman, gentle and sweet voice)Hello, welcome to VoxCPM2!", cfg_value=2.0, inference_timesteps=10, ) sf.write("voice_design.wav", wav, model.tts_model.sample_rate) ``` ### Controllable Voice Cloning ```python # Basic cloning wav = model.generate( text="This is a cloned voice generated by VoxCPM2.", reference_wav_path="speaker.wav", ) sf.write("clone.wav", wav, model.tts_model.sample_rate) # Cloning with style control wav = model.generate( text="(slightly faster, cheerful tone)This is a cloned voice with style control.", reference_wav_path="speaker.wav", cfg_value=2.0, inference_timesteps=10, ) sf.write("controllable_clone.wav", wav, model.tts_model.sample_rate) ``` ### Ultimate Cloning Provide both the reference audio and its exact transcript for maximum fidelity. Pass the same clip to both `reference_wav_path` and `prompt_wav_path` for highest similarity: ```python wav = model.generate( text="This is an ultimate cloning demonstration using VoxCPM2.", prompt_wav_path="speaker_reference.wav", prompt_text="The transcript of the reference audio.", reference_wav_path="speaker_reference.wav", ) sf.write("hifi_clone.wav", wav, model.tts_model.sample_rate) ``` ### Streaming ```python import numpy as np chunks = [] for chunk in model.generate_streaming(text="Streaming is easy with VoxCPM!"): chunks.append(chunk) wav = np.concatenate(chunks) sf.write("streaming.wav", wav, model.tts_model.sample_rate) ``` ## Model Details | Property | Value | |---|---| | Architecture | Tokenizer-free Diffusion Autoregressive (LocEnc → TSLM → RALM → LocDiT) | | Backbone | Based on MiniCPM-4, totally 2B parameters | | Audio VAE | AudioVAE V2 (asymmetric encode/decode, 16kHz in → 48kHz out) | | Training Data | 2M+ hours multilingual speech | | LM Token Rate | 6.25 Hz | | Max Sequence Length | 8192 tokens | | dtype | bfloat16 | | VRAM | ~8 GB | | RTF (RTX 4090) | ~0.30 (standard) / ~0.13 (Nano-vLLM) | ## Performance VoxCPM2 achieves state-of-the-art or competitive results on major zero-shot and controllable TTS benchmarks. See the [GitHub repo](https://github.com/OpenBMB/VoxCPM#-performance) for full benchmark tables (Seed-TTS-eval, CV3-eval, InstructTTSEval, MiniMax Multilingual Test). ## Fine-tuning VoxCPM2 supports both full SFT and LoRA fine-tuning with as little as 5–10 minutes of audio: ```bash # LoRA fine-tuning (recommended) python scripts/train_voxcpm_finetune.py \ --config_path conf/voxcpm_v2/voxcpm_finetune_lora.yaml # Full fine-tuning python scripts/train_voxcpm_finetune.py \ --config_path conf/voxcpm_v2/voxcpm_finetune_all.yaml ``` See the [Fine-tuning Guide](https://voxcpm.readthedocs.io/en/latest/finetuning/finetune.html) for full instructions. ## Limitations - Voice Design and Style Control results may vary between runs; generating 1–3 times is recommended to obtain the desired output. - Performance varies across languages depending on training data availability. - Occasional instability may occur with very long or highly expressive inputs. - **Strictly forbidden** to use for impersonation, fraud, or disinformation. AI-generated content should be clearly labeled. ## Citation ```bibtex @article{voxcpm2_2026, title = {VoxCPM2: Tokenizer-Free TTS for Multilingual Speech Generation, Creative Voice Design, and True-to-Life Cloning}, author = {VoxCPM Team}, journal = {GitHub}, year = {2026}, } @article{voxcpm2025, title = {VoxCPM: Tokenizer-Free TTS for Context-Aware Speech Generation and True-to-Life Voice Cloning}, author = {Zhou, Yixuan and Zeng, Guoyang and Liu, Xin and Li, Xiang and Yu, Renjie and Wang, Ziyang and Ye, Runchuan and Sun, Weiyue and Gui, Jiancheng and Li, Kehan and Wu, Zhiyong and Liu, Zhiyuan}, journal = {arXiv preprint arXiv:2509.24650}, year = {2025}, } ``` ## License Released under the [Apache-2.0](https://www.apache.org/licenses/LICENSE-2.0) license, free for commercial use. For production deployments, we recommend thorough testing and safety evaluation tailored to your use case.

# DuplexJev-32B-Para (v1.4)

📄 Paper: [arXiv:2610.02638](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02638) · Code: [github.com/adventists-ai/duplexjev](https://github.com/adventists-ai/duplexjev) · Release notes: [Japanese as a third language](https://github.com/adventists-ai/duplexjev/blob/main/research/2026-10-japanese.md) · [weak languages](https://github.com/adventists-ai/duplexjev/blob/main/research/2026-10-weak-languages.md) · Research notes: [hearing stress](https://github.com/adventists-ai/duplexjev/blob/main/research/2026-10-stress-understanding.md) · [keeping a speech-decision LLM able to talk](https://github.com/adventists-ai/duplexjev/blob/main/research/2026-10-chat-replay.md)

**The DuplexJev model that hears the most beyond the words.** On top of everything
[DuplexJev-32B-Turn](https://huggingface.co/adventists-ai/DuplexJev-32B-Turn) and
[DuplexJev-32B-Stress](https://huggingface.co/adventists-ai/DuplexJev-32B-Stress) do (spoken QA, gender, emotion,
turn-taking, stress and pauses), it also hears **laughter, breathing, coughs and sighs**, notices **how** someone is
talking (whispering, shouting, very fast or slow), and can tell, roughly as a person would, **whether two clips are
the same speaker**. Mandarin and English. Since v1.1 it also **holds a normal conversation**, multi-turn included.
**v1.2** adds **accent judgments** (English accents and Mandarin dialect regions) and much sharper **end-of-turn
detection right after the user pauses**: on LiveKit's eot-bench it now beats Smart Turn v3.2 in English and Chinese.
**v1.3** hears **stress** much better: on the public StressTest benchmark it goes from 72 to **85**, on StressPresso's
meaning questions from 69 to **89**, and on choosing the meaning a stressed word implies (DEBATE, held-out) from 85 to **93**, with the
other decisions about the same.
**v1.4** understands far more languages: **Japanese** error goes from 33 % to **12 %** (FLEURS) and from 38 % to
**11 %** on conversational Japanese, Korean and Vietnamese error falls to a quarter to a third of v1.3, Thai,
Arabic and Russian error by 30–40 %, and Mandarin conversational paralinguistics (laughter, breath, drawl, stutter …) are much sharper.

> **v1.4 (2026-10-22)** replaces v1.3 (2026-10-15): many more languages, Mandarin paralinguistics much better.
> Earlier versions stay available as revisions `v1.3`, `v1.2`, `v1.1` and `v1.0` (`--revision v1.3` in vLLM,
> `revision="v1.3"` in `from_pretrained`).

DuplexJev reads typed, closed-set decisions from speech as a **single-token distribution** of the LLM: zero decode
steps, many questions about the same clip in parallel. This repository is the complete model (Qwen3-ASR-0.6B encoder
+ connector + the language model of Qwen3-VL-32B, 33.0 B parameters, bf16; one 80 GB GPU).

**Which 32B to pick.** This one, for everything above.

## What changed

Starting from DuplexJev-32B-Turn we trained the connector and a new rank-16 LoRA on the LLM (merged here) for 4,000
steps. The mix is the 32B-Turn mix plus:

| added data | what it teaches |
|---|---|
| stress / pause detection (as in 32B-Stress: DEBATE, Stress-17K, TinyStress-15K, Expresso, neutral negatives) | which word is stressed, or none; where the pause is |
| speaker pairs (VoxCeleb1 dev, AISHELL-1, LibriSpeech, two-speaker mixtures) | same speaker or not; is this person in the clip |
| non-verbal sounds (VocalSound, NonVerbalSpeech-38K, NonverbalTTS, Expresso laughing) | is there laughter / breathing / a cough / a sigh / sniffing / throat clearing / a sneeze / crying …; negatives are cut from the same recordings away from the event |
| speaking style (EARS, Expresso whisper) | whispering, loud, fast, slow, high or low pitch, normal |
| spoken multiple-choice replay (ARC, OpenBookQA and CommonsenseQA train splits read by TTS) | keeps "answer the content" from being crowded out by "listen to the voice" |
| **v1.1:** conversation replay (spoken and typed user turns, up to 6 earlier turns as history; target = the original LLM's own reply) and in-house chat items | normal, full-length replies; trained with per-row loss averaging so long replies do not swamp the one-token decisions |
| **v1.2:** accents (VCTK, English Dialects, EdAcc, Common Voice accent labels, KeSpeech; held-out speakers kept for testing) | which accent: 19 English accents and 9 Mandarin dialect regions; native speaker or not; standard Mandarin or not; which English region |
| **v1.2:** end of turn right after a pause (otoSpeech-141h cut 0.2 s into each pause, with DualTurn labels; Smart Turn v3.2 training set) | finished vs. still talking / hesitating when the user has just gone quiet, the way a live voice agent has to decide |
| **v1.3:** the stress data re-balanced (more "which meaning does this stress imply" items, weight raised) and the gender data weighted ×2; no new corpora | choosing the meaning a stressed word implies; keeping gender where it was |
| **v1.4:** weak-language speech (ja, ko, vi, th, ar, ru: Emilia, Emilia-YODAS, YODAS2, Zeroth-Korean, VIVOS, FLEURS train, Common Voice; 162 k, labels re-checked with Qwen3-ASR-0.6B) + continuation (36 k) | transcribe and understand these languages |
| **v1.4:** Japanese speech (Emilia JA, Emilia-YODAS JA, Common Voice ja and other Japanese speech data; 358 k, re-checked) + Japanese continuation (20 k) | Japanese close to Chinese and English |
| **v1.4:** Mandarin conversational paralinguistics (licensed MagicData corpus, training speakers only; 42 k questions) | laughter, laughing while talking, breath, lip smack, sniff, cough, stressed word, drawl, which character is drawn out, stutter, sudden noise, unnatural pause, sentence emotion |
| **v1.4:** more emotion classes (surprise, fear, anxiety, excitement, encouragement, apologetic, playful) from CSEMOTIONS, EmotionTalk, DailyTalk, JL-Corpus, EMNS, Emozionalmente, SUBESCO | emotions beyond the basic four |

v1.4 was trained from v1.3 in four short stages (2,000 + 2,000 + 1,500 + 1,000 steps; connector + a new rank-16 LoRA
each time, merged here), replaying the full v1.3 mix in every stage; the last two stages raise the stress,
non-verbal, emotion and speaking-style replay ×1.5 each.

| **v1.4** | **11.6** | **7.6** | **14.6** | **18.0** | **19.4** | **6.9** | 3.8 | 0.0 | 3.5 | 7.0 | 5.3 |
| encoder ceiling (Qwen3-ASR-0.6B) | 7.0 | 2.7 | 7.8 | 5.1 | 16.7 | 7.8 | 2.0 | 1.3 | 3.4 | 6.2 | 5.6 |

**v1.4 11.1 / 13.0** (encoder 8.3 / 10.8).

question, P(finished) + P(backchannel); run with every eot-bench decision point (adapter
`benchmarks/turn_detection/eot_bench/duplexjev_ctx_adapter.py` on GitHub). `readout="act"` (`pipecat-duplexjev>=0.4`,
`livekit-plugins-duplexjev>=0.3`): question "What should the assistant do now?", P(reply now) + P(short
acknowledgement). Rows marked fast mode ask once per pause, at the 0.2 s score point.

**Pipecat [Smart Turn v3.2](https://huggingface.co/datasets/pipecat-ai/smart-turn-data-v3.2-test) test set**
(accuracy at threshold 0.5): v1.2 English 94.0% (Smart Turn v3.2: 94.7%), Chinese 91.1% (90.5%); v1.3 94.2% / 91.4%; DuplexJev-32B-Turn
65.2% / 84.6%. The Smart Turn v3.2 *training* set is in our training mix, so this is an in-distribution result.

## Serve with vLLM

```bash
pip install "vllm[audio]>=0.29" duplexjev-vllm
vllm serve adventists-ai/DuplexJev-32B-Para --max-model-len 4096
```

Prompt format and client are the same as for [DuplexJev-32B-Turn](https://huggingface.co/adventists-ai/DuplexJev-32B-Turn);
see [`examples/vllm_client.py`](https://github.com/adventists-ai/duplexjev/blob/main/examples/vllm_client.py). Examples:

```
The user said: <|audio|>

Is there laughter in this audio?

Options:
A. Yes
B. No

Answer with the letter only.
```

```
用户说：<|audio|>

除了说话，这段音频里还有哪种声音？

选项：
A. 叹气
B. 咳嗽
C. 笑声
D. 都没有

请只回答选项字母。
```

Always offer a "none" option for stress and non-verbal questions; the model was trained with it.

## Limitations

- Turn-taking, accent and same-speaker scores were not re-measured for v1.4.
- Thai and Arabic are still 2–3× the encoder's own error.
- Non-verbal training audio is mostly acted (radio drama, animation, studio recordings); in natural conversation the
  scores are lower (see the table).
- Breathing in natural Mandarin conversation is weak (AUC 0.56 in v1.2, 0.65 in v1.1, 0.78 in v1.0); acted / read
  speech is much better.
- Accent answers describe how someone sounds, not where they are from or who they are; accents are often mixed or
  ambiguous. Do not use them to make decisions about people.
- Asked about itself, it may describe abilities (seeing images, speaking) that this checkpoint does not have on its
  own: it takes speech and text and replies in text.
- Speaker judgments are coarse (EER 18–40%) and must not be used to identify or verify people.
- Emotion labels come from acted corpora; do not use the outputs to make decisions about individuals.

# DuplexJev-4B-Para (v1.3)

📄 Paper: [arXiv:2610.02638](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02638) · Code: [github.com/adventists-ai/duplexjev](https://github.com/adventists-ai/duplexjev) · Release notes: [Japanese as a third language](https://github.com/adventists-ai/duplexjev/blob/main/research/2026-10-japanese.md) · [weak languages](https://github.com/adventists-ai/duplexjev/blob/main/research/2026-10-weak-languages.md)

**The small DuplexJev that hears the most beyond the words, now with Japanese close to its Chinese and English.**

> **v1.3 (2026-10-22)** replaces v1.2 (2026-10-21). Earlier versions stay available as revisions `v1.2`, `v1.1` and
> `v1.0` (`--revision v1.2` in vLLM, `revision="v1.2"` in `from_pretrained`).

v1.2 brought Japanese from 60 % to 36 % error; v1.3 halves it again (FLEURS 17.2 %, conversational Japanese 13.1 %),
with Chinese and English unchanged.

Architecture: Qwen3-ASR-0.6B encoder + connector + Qwen3-4B, 4.2 B parameters, bf16, ~10 GB GPU memory.

## What changed

Continued from v1.2 in two stages (connector + a rank-64 LoRA on the LLM each time, merged here; 4,000 steps each),
the full v1.2 mix replayed, plus:

| added data | items | what it teaches |
|---|---:|---|
| Japanese speech: Emilia JA, Emilia-YODAS JA, Common Voice ja and other Japanese speech data | 358 k | transcribe; every label re-checked against Qwen3-ASR-0.6B, disagreeing clips dropped |
| Japanese continuation (text teacher: Qwen3-32B) | 20 k | understand, not just repeat |
| Mandarin conversational paralinguistics, second version (licensed MagicData corpus, training speakers only) | 42 k | adds stutter / repeated word, which character is drawn out, sudden noise, unnatural pause |

Japanese was weighted 15,000 in the first stage and 30,000 in the second.

## Results

Japanese (lower is better; FLEURS = median per-utterance character error on the test split; Emilia = a held-out Emilia
JA shard of conversational speech; CV = Common Voice ja test; 150 utterances each):

| | FLEURS ja | Emilia ja | Common Voice ja |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| v1.1 | 59.6 | 60.0 | 62.5 |
| v1.2 | 35.8 | 27.5 | 39.7 |
| **v1.3** | **17.2** | **13.1** | **20.3** |
| encoder ceiling (Qwen3-ASR-0.6B) | 7.0 | 8.3 | 10.8 |

FLEURS test, other languages (median word / character error):

| | ko | vi | th | ar | ru | zh | en |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| v1.2 | 20.3 | 41.3 | 33.3 | 58.6 | 36.4 | 9.4 | 5.6 |
| **v1.3** | 18.8 | 38.4 | 33.0 | 57.1 | 34.5 | 8.2 | 5.3 |

```bash
pip install "vllm[audio]>=0.29" duplexjev-vllm
vllm serve adventists-ai/DuplexJev-4B-Para --max-model-len 4096
# previous version: add --revision v1.2
```

Decision prompts are the same as for [DuplexJev-4B-Turn](https://huggingface.co/adventists-ai/DuplexJev-4B-Turn); see [`examples/vllm_client.py`](https://github.com/adventists-ai/duplexjev/blob/main/examples/vllm_client.py). Always offer a "none" option for stress and non-verbal questions. For
conversation, send the user audio as the user turn (`<|audio|>`) with ordinary chat history and sample as usual.

Compact English speech synthesis and voice enrollment models, converted and

Nodes on GitHub · All samples · Qwen3-ASR for the transcripts · The original model

**[Fish Audio Drama 3](https://huggingface.co/fishaudio/drama-3)**, converted for the native ComfyUI nodes of **[ComfyUI-Drama3](https://github.com/PedroMarinhoDev/ComfyUI-Drama3)**: a 35B text-to-speech model for voice cloning, dialogue and inline cues such as `[sighs]` or `[whispers]`, running **on cards from 8 GB**. 90% of the model is routed experts and each audio frame uses only 8 of the 256 in a layer, so the nodes keep the experts in system RAM and a cache of the ones in use on the GPU. Each file holds the whole model in one file; the codec is separate. Built with Fish Audio. ## Samples No real person is cloned here: the first three clone voices the model made up from a single line, the rest are voices it invents from the prompt alone. Drama 3 FP8, experts in RAM, temperature 1.0, top_p 0.9, top_k 30 (the nodes now default to top_k 0, as Fish Audio's Space does: top_k 30 made some takes fall silent and drop a sentence). **[More on the demo page →](https://pedromarinhodev.github.io/ComfyUI-Drama3/)** **Voice cloning**: the source clip, a voice the model made up from one line, then a new line in that voice > The lighthouse keeper climbed the last step, set her lantern on the sill, and watched the storm roll in across the bay. Somewhere below, a bell began to ring. **Inline cues** > [whispers] Don't move. I think it heard us. [pause] [sighs] Oh, it's only the cat. [laughs] You should have seen your face. **Two speakers** > <|speaker:0|> Did you remember the tickets?
> <|speaker:1|> [laughs] I thought you had them!
> <|speaker:0|> [sighs] Then we're watching the concert from the parking lot. **Five speakers**, no voices given: the model casts all five > <|speaker:0|> [dramatic dungeon master] You enter the dark cave. A dragon sleeps on a pile of gold.
> <|speaker:1|> [brave, too loud] I attack the dragon! … **Singing** > [singing, grand operatic] Oh toast, my golden toast, you're the bread I love the most! [singing softly] Crispy edges, warm and brown, finest slice in all the town. … **Portuguese** > [Brazilian football fan, building tension, Portuguese] Vai, vai, vai, vai! Ele passou por um, passou por dois, [shouting] olha o chute! … ## Files **Start with FP8**: it holds Fish Audio's own expert weights, byte for byte, next to the checkpoint's bf16 layers. The int8 file is the same size, measured as close to the original, and ran 14–17% faster than FP8 on an RTX 3090: the nodes turn FP8 experts into bf16 each time they run, while int8 experts run as int8. Take a smaller file when your system RAM is short of the FP8 file's ~48 GB. Every model file needs the codec. | File | Size | Experts | System RAM | Notes | |---|---|---|---|---| | [`drama3_fp8experts_bf16.safetensors`](drama3_fp8experts_bf16.safetensors) | 38.6 GB | FP8, as Fish Audio ships them | ~48 GB | the original weights | | [`drama3_int8experts_bf16.safetensors`](drama3_int8experts_bf16.safetensors) | 38.7 GB | int8 ConvRot | ~48 GB | faster than FP8 on the 3090; no silent take in 12 cloned test takes | | [`drama3_w6a8experts_bf16.safetensors`](drama3_w6a8experts_bf16.safetensors) | 32.7 GB | W6A8 | ~40 GB | no silent take in 16 cloned test takes | | [`drama3_w4a8experts_bf16.safetensors`](drama3_w4a8experts_bf16.safetensors) | 24.6 GB | W4A8 | ~32 GB | falls silent more often with real voice clips | | [`drama3_codec.safetensors`](drama3_codec.safetensors) | 1.6 GB | | | the original codec, fp32 | ## Quick start 1. **Install the nodes**: clone [ComfyUI-Drama3](https://github.com/PedroMarinhoDev/ComfyUI-Drama3) into `ComfyUI/custom_nodes` and restart ComfyUI. Nothing to `pip install`. 2. **Download** a model file into `models/diffusion_models` and `drama3_codec.safetensors` into `models/vae`. For transcripts, add `qwen3_asr_1.7b_bf16.safetensors` from [Qwen3-ASR-ComfyUI](https://huggingface.co/PedroMarinhoDev/Qwen3-ASR-ComfyUI) to `models/asr`, and for the Drama 3 Editor's word-by-word captions, `qwen3_forced_aligner_0.6b_bf16.safetensors` from the same repository. ```bash hf download PedroMarinhoDev/Drama-3-ComfyUI drama3_fp8experts_bf16.safetensors --local-dir ComfyUI/models/diffusion_models hf download PedroMarinhoDev/Drama-3-ComfyUI drama3_codec.safetensors --local-dir ComfyUI/models/vae hf download PedroMarinhoDev/Qwen3-ASR-ComfyUI qwen3_asr_1.7b_bf16.safetensors --local-dir ComfyUI/models/asr hf download PedroMarinhoDev/Qwen3-ASR-ComfyUI qwen3_forced_aligner_0.6b_bf16.safetensors --local-dir ComfyUI/models/asr ``` 3. **Open the workflow** `example_workflows/drama3_voice_clone.json` from the pack, pick a few seconds of clean speech, write your text, run. 4. **Edit the take** (optional): the **Drama 3 Editor** node, in place of Decode, shows the take on a timeline with one track per voice and captions that follow the words; it shortens long pauses, spaces out lines that run into each other, flags lines that may have lost words, and cuts. For dialogue, give each speaker a voice: the voice in slot `voiceN` speaks for `<|speaker:N|>`. ## Requirements and speed | | | |---|---| | GPU | NVIDIA, 8 GB of VRAM or more with experts in RAM (tested: RTX 4090 and RTX 3090; 12 GB and 8 GB simulated on the 3090) | | System RAM | the model file plus ~8 GB | | ComfyUI | v0.40 or newer | Drama 3 makes 21.5 audio frames per second of speech, so 46 ms per frame is real time. Experts in RAM, a cloned voice, ~9 s of speech, prompt pass included, measured on 2026-10-15 with an Intel Core i9-14900K (the held rows on 2026-10-14). One frame at a time, decoding waits on the CPU: int8 runs at the same 69 ms per frame on both GPUs, and a CPU with slower cores adds to these times: | GPU | File | Expert cache | ms per frame | |---|---|---|---| | RTX 4090 (PCIe 4.0 ×8) | W4A8 | 16 GB | 52 | | RTX 4090 (PCIe 4.0 ×8) | int8 | 16 GB | 69 | | RTX 3090 (PCIe 4.0 ×8) | int8 | 16 GB | 69 | | RTX 3090 (PCIe 4.0 ×8) | FP8 | 16 GB | 84 | | RTX 3090 held to 12 GB | FP8 | automatic | 137 | | RTX 3090 held to 8 GB | FP8 | automatic | 214 | ## How these files were made From [fishaudio/drama-3](https://huggingface.co/fishaudio/drama-3) with the pack's `tools/convert.py`: - **FP8**: the routed experts' FP8 bytes and 128×128 block scales copied unchanged, gate and up projections fused. - **int8 / W6A8 / W4A8**: the experts dequantized from FP8 in fp32 and requantized, in ComfyUI's comfy_kitchen formats: int8 ConvRot (per-channel int8 after a rotation in groups of 256), or 6-bit or 4-bit codebook weights with int8 activations; relative weight error 0.83%, 2.1% and 7.3%. - **Every file**: the attention, DeltaNet, shared-expert and codebook-decoder layers are the checkpoint's own bf16; the LM head keeps only the rows generation samples from (end of speech and the 4096 semantic codes). - **Codec**: Fish Audio's S2-Pro codec as shipped with Drama 3, weight norm folded in, fp32. Against Fish Audio's own PyTorch code, with the same frames forced, the main token's distribution differs by a KL of 0.004–0.008 nats with the FP8 and int8 files, the noise of bf16 arithmetic. ## License These Fish Audio Materials are licensed under the Fish Audio Community License, Version 1.0.
